summary:
The Curiosity Project is an educational website featuring interactive game elements, such as assembling a Mars rover with various configurations and landing it on Mars.

In addition to the game, the website features materials on NASA’s lunar and Martian missions, drawing on open sources and real images of the spacecraft. Through this combined format, we give teenagers the opportunity to get a taste of space engineering and real science.

We believe our project can play a huge role in sparking the next generation’s interest in space, thanks to the accessible format of the game mechanics and the engaging information that teenagers will find easier to process. Additionally, the project promotes NASA’s open archives, which directly supports youth education and the development of citizen science.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? Curiosity: The Legacy Archive is a bilingual (EN/RU) web platform with two parts: 1) an interactive 3D archive of 16 completed NASA missions on Mars and the Moon detailing scientific discoveries, spacecraft hardware, and flight software; 2) Mission Lab, an engineering simulator where users build a custom rover within a budget across 7,776 component combinations and run a physics-based Mars landing.

What benefits does it have? It consolidates fragmented NASA Science and NASA PDS records into a fast, clutter-free interface and turns passive reading into hands-on STEM practice by letting users balance rover mass, touchdown impact limits, and payload budgets.

What is the intended impact of the project? It reframes inactive spacecraft on Mars and the Moon from abandoned hardware into enduring scientific monuments, inspiring students to explore aerospace engineering, planetary physics, and flight software through an accessible browser tool.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), JSON, WebGL / Three.js, and HTML5 Canvas for 3D planetary globes and landing physics, developed in Visual Studio Code with Git and deployed on Vercel, using 100% official open data from NASA Science, NASA PDS, NASA Image and Video Library, and NASA/JPL Photojournal.

How is your project creative? It connects a dual-world 3D archive (Mars and Moon) directly to an interactive JPL-style workshop: users study how historic spacecraft and their flight software (C/C++, VxWorks, BAE RAD750) succeeded or failed, then immediately test those same mechanical choices (Rocker-bogie suspension, thermal shields, and a Hard Mode with a 3% engine failure risk) on their own rover.

What factors did your team consider? We focused on 100% verified official NASA HTTPS sources, a clean dark-space UI with concise 3-metric mission summaries, a balance between accurate landing physics and accessible gameplay (quick presets plus NASA fact pop-ups), fast browser performance, and full English/Russian localization.
